Assuming rank 1 is highest-scoring and the 16 are drawn uniformly from ranks 33–80, this sampler makes negatives **easier in expectation than uniform-64**. The remaining 80 are themselves uniform; discarding their hardest 32 leaves the easiest 60%. The selected component’s expected descending rank is 56.5 versus 40.5 under uniform sampling. Thus the final set is 75% uniform plus 25% easy-biased—not semi-hard enrichment. This is an order-statistic deduction, not an experimental result; selecting the first 16 within that window changes its magnitude, not its direction.

A difficulty-increasing rank window must favor an upper-scoring portion of the uniform pool while skipping its extreme top—for example, ranks 9–24 of 80, mixed with uniform negatives. Those cutoffs are illustrative hyperparameters, not established optima. Alternatively, select negatives just below the positive’s score. [SimANS](https://aclanthology.org/2022.emnlp-industry.56.pdf) supports positive-relative ambiguous sampling with softmax contrastive training in dense retrieval, but does not establish these cutoffs for BERT4Rec. Skipping top ranks is only a false-negative-risk heuristic: rank alone cannot identify latent positives. Exclude known training positives; never consult held-out labels.

For candidate cross-entropy, each negative’s logit gradient equals its candidate-softmax probability, so high-scoring negatives already dominate updates. [Sampled-softmax research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.02327) analyzes this implicit hard-negative emphasis; changing the sampler also changes the uncorrected training objective. [Hard-BPR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19276) instead modifies the **pairwise BPR loss** to reduce false-negative influence under hard sampling. Its robustness results do not establish protection for ordinary 64-negative cross-entropy or this rank window. Validate hardness and macro HR@10 empirically; do not equate easier sampling with demonstrated false-negative protection.
